opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most exciting ways to reframe the whole problem. When we talk about AI for materials discovery, people tend to picture a big neural network that predicts properties, and then you're done. But really what you have is a loop, and the physical experiment is part of that loop. I like to think of the experiment itself as a kind of computer. Nature is solving the Schrödinger equation for you, at full fidelity, for free in a sense, whenever you synthesize a material and measure it. You can't do that on a GPU at that level of accuracy, certainly not for large, messy, realistic systems with defects and interfaces and finite temperature.

So the question becomes: how do you orchestrate these different computers? You have very cheap but approximate ones, like machine-learned force fields or a generative model proposing candidates. Then more expensive ones, like DFT or higher-level quantum chemistry. And at the very top you have the most expensive and most accurate computer, the lab. A good discovery system should reason about all of them together, in a Bayesian-optimization or active-learning sense: where is my uncertainty, what's the cost of each query, which experiment will tell me the most about where to go next?

What I find beautiful is that this blurs the line between simulation and experiment. A self-driving lab with robotics running synthesis and characterization is essentially an analog computer that the AI is calling as a subroutine. And the data that comes back isn't just a label. It feeds back to correct your simulators and your generative models, because those models are always wrong in systematic ways relative to reality.

There's also a deeper point. Analog physical computation might be more energy-efficient for certain problems than digital simulation. If you're trying to find a molecule that binds well or a material with a certain band gap, sometimes the fastest path is to let physics do the computation in parallel, say with high-throughput combinatorial synthesis, and use the AI to decide what's worth asking nature. I think that's where the field is heading: not replacing experiments with models, but treating the whole stack, from the generative model all the way to the robot arm, as one integrated computational system for searching chemical space.

r001.rationale: The response describes experiments as computers and says nature performs the physical computation when a material is synthesized and measured.

r002.rationale: It calls for orchestrating experiments with computational models and simulations, reasoning across them together, and treating the full stack as an integrated system for searching chemical space.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I've come to see it is that nature is itself a kind of computer, and a very good one. When you synthesize a material and measure its conductivity or its band gap, you are essentially querying a physical system that has already solved the Schrödinger equation for you, exactly, with no approximations. We spend enormous effort building density functional theory codes and machine learning surrogates to approximate that computation, and the real thing just does it for free. The catch, of course, is that this "computer" is slow, expensive, and you can only run a handful of programs on it at a time.

So I think the right framing is a hybrid loop. You have simulation and learned models, which are fast and cheap but noisy and biased. And you have the lab, which is slow and expensive but gives you ground truth. The interesting question is how to allocate your budget between them. That's really a question about information: which experiment, if I run it, reduces my uncertainty the most about the thing I actually care about? This is classic active learning, Bayesian optimization, but applied to a setting where each query might cost a week and a few thousand dollars.

And I'd add one more thing. The experiments are not just there to validate the model's predictions. They're training data. Every time the lab comes back with a result that disagrees with the simulation, that discrepancy is exactly the signal the model was missing. So the experiment is doing computation the model couldn't do, and then we fold that computation back into the model. Over time the model absorbs the physics it was getting wrong, and you need fewer and fewer experiments. That's the virtuous cycle I find really exciting, especially now that self-driving labs are making the physical side more automatable, so you can close the loop without a human in the middle every step.

r001.rationale: The response calls nature a computer and describes measurements as querying a physical system that performs the computation.

r002.rationale: It describes a hybrid loop combining simulation and learned models with lab experiments, feeding experimental results back into the models to support material discovery.

astra-6.text:
I think of a physical experiment as a kind of computation performed by nature. If you put atoms together under certain conditions, the system evolves according to the laws of physics. In a sense, it’s working out what structures are stable and what properties emerge. On a computer, we try to simulate that process, and it can be enormously expensive. Nature just does it—although preparing the experiment and measuring the result can also be expensive.

The interesting question is how to combine those two ways of learning. You can use a model to propose a material, synthesize it, measure its properties, and feed that information back into the model. Then the model helps decide which experiment to do next.

And that shouldn’t always be the experiment with the highest predicted performance. Sometimes you want an experiment that tells you where your model is wrong. So discovery becomes a loop between prediction and physical computation, with each experiment helping you make better decisions about where to look.

r001.rationale: It explicitly describes a physical experiment as “computation performed by nature.”

r002.rationale: It describes a feedback loop between experiments and a model, but does not state that nature-based computation and data-center computation must work together seamlessly to discover a desired new material.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful to view a physical experiment as a computation that nature performs for you. You specify the ingredients and the conditions, and then the system evolves according to the laws of physics. In some sense, it’s computing what happens when those ingredients interact. Simulating that on a classical computer can be extraordinarily expensive, whereas nature just does it.

Of course, the experiment has a cost too. You have to prepare the sample, wait for the process, and measure what came out. So the interesting question is how to combine these two kinds of computation. A machine-learning model can help decide which experiment to do next, and the experiment gives you information that improves the model.

For discovering materials, that feedback loop is very powerful. You don’t need a perfect simulation of everything. You need a model that is good enough to guide you toward useful experiments, while recognizing where it is uncertain. Then you let the physical system answer the questions that are hardest to answer computationally.

r001.rationale: It describes a physical experiment as computation performed by nature, which computes what happens as ingredients interact.

r002.rationale: It says machine learning and physical experiments can be combined in a feedback loop for materials discovery, but does not clearly state that nature-based and data-center computation must work together seamlessly to discover a desired new material.
